#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP)
Description: The Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP) is a nationally representative longitudinal survey that provides comprehensive information on the dynamics of income, employment, household composition, and government program participation. SIPP is also a leading source of data on economic well-being, family dynamics, education, wealth, health insurance, child care, and food security. The survey interviews individuals for several years and provides monthly data about changes in household and family composition and economic circumstances over time.
URL: https://census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp.html

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP)
Description: The Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP) is a nationally representative longitudinal survey that provides comprehensive information on the dynamics of income, employment, household composition, and government program participation. SIPP is also a leading source of data on economic well-being, family dynamics, education, wealth, health insurance, child care, and food security. The survey interviews individuals for several years and provides monthly data about changes in household and family composition and economic circumstances over time.
URL: https://census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp.html

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research the Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP) comprehensively. Let me gather information from multiple angles.Let me gather a few more details on users, statutory uses, and preservation/archival aspects.# Research Report: Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP)

## Verification of Your Information

Your dataset description is **accurate**. The title, description, and URL all match the official Census Bureau program page (https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp.html). The description language is drawn directly from the Bureau's own program overview. A few clarifying details and a great deal of additional context follow below.

---

## 1. Basic Identification

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Title** | Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP) |
| **Publisher / Producer** | U.S. Census Bureau, U.S. Department of Commerce |
| **Type** | Nationally representative longitudinal (panel) household survey; public-use microdata plus published tabulations |
| **Population** | U.S. civilian, noninstitutionalized population; all household members, with individuals interviewed directly (historically ages 15+) |
| **Frequency** | Continuous panels since 1983; since the 2014 redesign, annual interviews covering a 12-month calendar-year reference period, with data released roughly annually (e.g., 2025 SIPP covers January–December 2024) |
| **Landing page** | https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp.html |
| **Data files** | https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/data/datasets.html and the FTP-style tree at https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/ |
| **Contact** | SIPP Coordination and Outreach Staff, census.sipp@census.gov |

---

## 2. Authority and Mandate

- **Statutory authority:** SIPP is conducted under **Title 13, United States Code, Section 182**, which authorizes the Census Bureau to conduct surveys on demographic and economic subjects "as necessary to furnish current data." Title 13 also carries the Bureau's strict **confidentiality protections** — responses may be used only for statistical purposes, are protected from disclosure, and are exempt from subpoena/FOIA in identifiable form.
- **Response is voluntary** (unlike the decennial census and ACS).
- **Paperwork Reduction Act clearance:** Like all federal surveys, SIPP operates under OMB information-collection approval, renewed periodically through Federal Register notices with public comment periods. These notices (e.g., the 2023 notice covering the 2024 collection and the August 2026 notice covering a planned 2027 field test) are important primary documents for tracking changes to the survey's design and sample.
- **Downstream statutory mandates:** While Title 13 authorizes collection, SIPP data are *required inputs* for other legally mandated products. Notably, SIPP is the principal data source for congressionally mandated annual reporting on welfare dependence and program participation (stemming from the 1996 welfare reform law, PRWORA), and it feeds models used by SSA, CBO, and USDA to cost out and evaluate benefit programs. This is a key point for advocates: cutting SIPP degrades the government's ability to fulfill other statutory reporting obligations.

---

## 3. History and Provenance

- **Origins (1975–1981):** SIPP grew out of the **Income Survey Development Program (ISDP)**, initiated in 1975 by the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare (HEW) in collaboration with the Census Bureau. Dissatisfaction with the Current Population Survey's annual, cross-sectional, retrospective income measurement drove the effort. Field tests ran in 1978 (~2,000 households) and 1979 (~8,200 households).
- **Near-death and rescue (1981–1983):** HEW lost ISDP funding in 1981 and the survey appeared stillborn. A 1982 rescue effort by the Census Bureau director, executive-branch staff, and Congress restored funding — the original plan had been SSA sponsorship with shared costs.
- **Launch (October 1983):** The first (1984) panel interviewed over 20,000 households, with re-interviews every four months over a 32-month period. New overlapping panels launched each February from 1985–1993 (17 panels total across the survey's history).
- **1993 CNSTAT review / 1996 redesign:** At the Bureau's request, the National Research Council's Committee on National Statistics reviewed SIPP (*The Future of the Survey of Income and Program Participation*, Citro & Kalton, 1993). The resulting 1996 redesign created a single larger four-year (48-month) panel, introduced **computer-assisted interviewing (CAI)**, and oversampled high-poverty areas. The launch was delayed to April 1996 by the 1995–96 government shutdowns; the 1996 welfare reform law (PRWORA) then forced mid-panel questionnaire changes (AFDC → TANF).
- **2006 crisis and Re-engineered SIPP:** Facing imminent cancellation in 2006, SIPP was saved by stakeholder advocacy, but redesigned to cut costs and burden. The new **SIPP-EHC** instrument shifted from a 4-month to a **12-month reference period** using an **Event History Calendar (EHC)** to aid recall. First interviews: February 2014; annual data files from 2018 onward.
- **Recent stressors (2020–present):** COVID-19 drove response-rate collapse (from 68% for the 2017 panel to roughly 37% in 2022) and a 2023 user note warning of "insufficient geographic coverage and unit nonresponse." Rising collection costs against flat appropriations forced a **sample cut from ~53,000 to 35,000 housing units** beginning with the 2023/2024 collections. The FY2026 President's budget and House CJS appropriations bill proposed cutting **$40 million** from the Census budget line containing SIPP, with the administration signaling a "sharply reduced" version reliant on administrative records. An **August 2026 Federal Register notice** announced plans for a **2027 field test in lieu of a national collection** using the questionnaires and systems in place since 2014 — i.e., the future of the full national survey is actively uncertain as of this writing.

---

## 4. Content and Methodology

**Core content (person-month level):**
- Income from dozens of sources (earnings, Social Security, SSI, TANF, SNAP, WIC, unemployment insurance, workers' comp, veterans' benefits, child support, pensions, investment income, school meals, energy assistance)
- Employment and labor force activity, including job spells and monthly transitions
- Household and family composition changes (including children moving between caregivers' homes — a uniquely valuable feature)
- Health insurance coverage, disability, education
- Wealth, assets and liabilities; retirement accounts; medical and jointly held debt
- Child care arrangements and costs; food security/material hardship items

**Methodological features data users must know:**
- **Structure:** The modern public-use file is **person-month level** — each individual can have up to 12 records per annual file; household variables are replicated across members, and spell-level variables across months within a spell.
- **Weights:** Calendar-year weights, **240 replicate weights** (for variance estimation), and **longitudinal weights** for 2-, 3-, and 4-year cohorts spanning the overlapping panels. Choosing the correct weight is a common user error; the Bureau publishes a "Guide to Selecting Weights."
- **Overlap:** Since 2014, panels overlap so that cross-sectional annual estimates combine multiple panel cohorts.
- **EHC design:** The Event History Calendar improves recall but makes the data structure ("autobiographical" spell-based reporting) more complex than typical surveys.

---

## 5. Data Products and Access

**Public-use products (free):**
- **Microdata** in SAS, Stata, and pipe-delimited text (.zip), with data dictionaries, schemas, and **Python/Pandas and R input examples** — notably preservation- and open-science-friendly
- Replicate weight files and longitudinal weight files
- **Complete technical documentation**: Users' Guides, release notes, user notes (data-quality caveats — essential reading), data primer, crosswalks between years, variable name change summaries (2014–2025), online codebook
- **Published tables**: detailed program-receipt tables (Social Security, TANF, SNAP, WIC, SSI, retirement income, UI, school meals, VA benefits, child support) and the P-70 Current Population Reports series
- **Data tools**: Census Microdata Access Tool (MDAT, in beta) for custom tabulations/extracts without downloading full files
- **Historical files**: All panels back to 1984 remain downloadable from census.gov/www2.census.gov, organized by panel and wave (core files, topical modules, full-panel longitudinal files)

**Restricted/enhanced products:**
- **SIPP Synthetic Beta (SSB)**: fully synthesized microdata linking nine SIPP panels (1984–2008) to SSA/IRS W-2 and benefit records, produced with Cornell, SSA, and IRS — designed to provide access to linked-data relationships without confidentiality risk
- **FSRDC access**: Internal (un-truncated) SIPP and SIPP linked to administrative records are available to researchers with approved projects in Federal Statistical Research Data Centers

**Third-party archives (preservation-relevant):**
- **ICPSR** maintains a SIPP series (e.g., ICPSR 8317 for the 1984 panel; ICPSR 8903 Health-Wealth Merged File) with DOIs and curated preservation
- **NBER** historically redistributed SIPP (1984–2001) in SAS/SPSS/Stata; it has discontinued maintenance now that Census provides multi-format files directly, but its archived files persist
- **CEPR** provides uniform extraction programs (Stata) for the 1990–2008 panels
- Older documentation references the retired DataFerrett tool and legacy FTP paths — a caution that access infrastructure has changed repeatedly over the survey's life

---

## 6. Typical Users

- **Federal agencies and modelers:** SSA's **MINT** dynamic microsimulation model (SIPP matched to Social Security records); **CBO** simulation models; USDA Economic Research Service and Food and Nutrition Service (including the **MATH SIPP+** SNAP eligibility model with Mathematica); HHS/ASPE analyses of safety-net participation and "benefit cliffs"
- **Congressional and legal mandates:** annual welfare-dependence and program-participation reporting to Congress
- **Academic researchers:** economics, sociology, public policy, demography, public health — SIPP underpins landmark work on welfare reform, poverty dynamics, SNAP participation, minimum wage effects, wealth inequality, health insurance dynamics, and student debt
- **Policy organizations and advocates:** CBPP, Urban Institute, the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights, and The Census Project, all of which have mobilized publicly in defense of SIPP funding and sample size
- **State policy analysts:** state identifiers (in appropriate files) allow evaluation of state variation in jointly administered programs like Medicaid and TANF

---

## 7. Benefits to the Public

1. **Unique measurement capability:** SIPP is the *only* nationally representative survey of its size that tracks monthly income, program participation, and household change longitudinally — including **duration of benefit receipt** (spells), which cross-sectional surveys like the CPS cannot measure.
2. **Policy costing and eligibility simulation:** Its monthly income data let policymakers estimate how changing an asset limit, recertification period, or eligibility rule would affect costs and caseloads for SNAP, SSI, Medicaid, WIC, TANF, and school meals. No proposed "administrative-records-only" replacement replicates this.
3. **Family-level realism:** It follows children across caregivers' households and captures multiple-program participation (e.g., ~90% of children on SNAP receive at least one other form of assistance), enabling analysis of the safety net as families actually experience it.
4. **Program evaluation after major reforms:** SIPP was explicitly designed to, and did, measure the effects of the 1996 welfare reform, and remains the benchmark for evaluating subsequent program changes.
5. **Transparency and accountability:** Free public microdata with strong documentation let independent researchers verify and extend official statistics.

---

## 8. Risks and Preservation Considerations (for Preservationists and Data Librarians)

This is where your dataset is currently most vulnerable:

- **Active funding threat:** A proposed $40 million cut (FY2026 budget and House CJS bill) and an administration vision of replacing survey content with unspecified administrative-records linkages. Watchdogs (CBPP, The Census Project) assess this would destroy SIPP's signature monthly longitudinal content.
- **Possible collection hiatus:** The August 2026 Federal Register notice proposes a **2027 field test "in lieu of a national collection"** — meaning there may be a gap year in national data, breaking a series that runs continuously since 1983.
- **Quality erosion already underway:** Sample cut of ~34% (53,000 → 35,000 housing units), response rates near 37%, and official user notes cautioning about 2022 data reliability. Community comments (including from former Census division chiefs) warn of nonresponse bias and loss of subgroup/geographic reliability.
- **Format longevity is decent but fragmented:** Current releases in open-ish formats (pipe-delimited text with schemas) plus SAS/Stata; but older panels exist in era-specific layouts (rectangular core files, topical module files, "full panel" files) with wave-specific documentation. The 1989 panel famously lacks a full-panel file, and some 1989 Wave 2 topical modules were never processed — provenance gaps already exist in the historical record.
- **Access churn:** DataFerrett is retired; NBER's mirror is unmaintained; MDAT is in beta; legacy FTP URLs in old documentation are dead links. A preservation strategy should capture: (1) microdata in the open pipe-delimited format with schemas, (2) all Users' Guides, user notes, data dictionaries, and crosswalks, (3) the SSB synthetic files, and (4) published tables. ICPSR's curated copies provide some redundancy, and community archives (e.g., DataLumos-style efforts and IPUMS-adjacent projects) are worth monitoring given the political environment.
- **Disclosure avoidance evolution:** A 2024 National Academies report, *A Roadmap for Disclosure Avoidance in SIPP*, signals coming changes to what is released publicly (more suppression, synthesis, or FSRDC-only access). Files downloaded today may be richer than files available tomorrow — an argument for proactive capture.

---

## 9. Key Documents for Your Research File

1. SIPP Introduction & History: https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/about/sipp-introduction-history.html
2. Current Users' Guides (e.g., 2025): https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/guidance/users-guide.html
3. Citro & Kalton (1993), *The Future of the Survey of Income and Program Participation* (CNSTAT/National Academies)
4. National Academies, *A Roadmap for Disclosure Avoidance in the Survey of Income and Program Participation*
5. CBPP (Sept. 2025), "Federal Data Are Disappearing as Statistical Agencies Face Budget Cuts and Political Pressure"
6. Federal Register (Aug. 7, 2026), SIPP 2027 field test OMB submission notice
7. The Census Project coverage of SIPP funding and the field test (thecensusproject.org)
8. Leadership Conference sign-on comments on the SIPP sample cut (civilrights.org)
9. SIPP Synthetic Beta documentation: https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/guidance/sipp-synthetic-beta-data-product.html
10. ICPSR SIPP series: https://www.icpsr.umich.edu/web/ICPSR/series/135

---

## Summary Assessment

SIPP is a flagship federal longitudinal dataset with a 40+ year continuous series, Title 13 authority and confidentiality protection, unusually rich monthly microdata on income and safety-net participation, free public distribution in multiple formats with strong documentation, and deep embeddedness in federal microsimulation, statutory reporting, and academic research. It is also, as of this writing, one of the most politically and fiscally endangered major federal surveys — facing a proposed $40M cut, a shrunken sample, collapsing response rates, and a planned 2027 field test that may interrupt national data collection. For preservationists, this combination of high value and high risk makes SIPP a priority candidate for proactive archiving of both current and historical files and their documentation.

I'll research the current status of SIPP across each rubric dimension before making my assessment.Let me verify a few more points on data release timeliness, historical file integrity, and administration policy statements.# SIPP Dataset Risk Assessment

**Assessment date context:** This assessment reflects developments through late 2026, including the enacted FY2026 appropriations (P.L. 119-74, signed January 23, 2026), the August 7, 2026 Federal Register notice on the 2027 SIPP field test, and the July 15, 2026 release of 2025 SIPP data.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence for "No Known Issue":**
- The Census Bureau's datasets page continues to offer the complete historical series: "Access SIPP data by year (2018–2025) or panel/wave (1984–2014)" — all 40+ years of panels, waves, topical modules, and full-panel files remain downloadable from census.gov and www2.census.gov (verified August 2026).
- Redundant curated copies exist at ICPSR (with DOIs), NBER, and CEPR, reducing single-point-of-failure risk.
- No reports of historical SIPP files being removed, altered, or placed behind access restrictions since January 2025.

**Evidence for elevated risk:**
- No files have been removed, but structural weaknesses noted in prior research: the 1989 panel lacks a full-panel file; some 1989 Wave 2 topical modules were never processed; legacy FTP links and DataFerrett access are dead. These are pre-existing provenance gaps, not new removals.
- The planned 2024 National Academies disclosure-avoidance roadmap could eventually lead to withdrawal and re-release of historical public-use files with more suppression — a theoretical future risk, not a current one.

**Assessment: No Known Issue.** Historical data remain fully accessible and unaltered. Preservationists should nonetheless capture copies now given risks identified below.

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence for "High Risk":**
- **Collection skip formally announced.** The August 7, 2026 Federal Register notice (91 FR 51147) states the Census Bureau will conduct "a field test of SIPP in calendar year 2027… **in lieu of a national collection** using the questionnaires, systems, and processes in place since 2014." This is an officially published plan to skip the national collection — a direct hit on the rubric's "collection or publication skipped" criterion. It breaks an unbroken national series running since 1983 and creates a gap in the annual reference-year series.
- The field test ICR (OMB Control No. 0607-1000) is a *new* collection request for only ~6,000 respondents; the future of the existing national ICR beyond 2026 is unclear.
- The FY2026 President's Budget proposed cutting SIPP's account by $40M and "did not outline SIPP's potential transition nor clarify if the program will continue under its current name" (Census Project, June 30, 2025).
- The Bureau's own modernization webinars describe a timeline "conditional on budget and OMB approval," with full-scale testing pushed to 2028 — leaving national production resumption uncertain.

**Evidence for "Moderate Risk" (mitigating):**
- Data releases have remained on schedule: 2024 SIPP released July 24, 2025; 2025 SIPP released July 15, 2026 — consistent with the established annual July pattern. No publication has yet been missed.
- Congress rejected the proposed $40M cut in the enacted FY2026 bill; the Current Surveys and Programs account received $318.5M (only –3.2% vs. FY2025), and the bill was signed with a positive Statement of Administration Policy.

**Assessment: High Risk.** Although releases to date have been punctual and Congress restored most funding, the Bureau has formally announced that national collection will be skipped in 2027. A planned, published collection skip meets the High Risk definition squarely.

---

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence for "High Risk" (reductions already occurred):**
- **Sample size reductions:** Wave 1 eligible households fell from 44,870 (2018 panel) to 12,266 (2024 panel) — a ~73% decline in per-panel intake following the 2023 cut from ~53,000 to ~35,000 housing units.
- **Response-rate collapse:** Weighted response rates fell from 68% (2017 panel) to 36.9% (2022 panel), recovering only partially to ~46% (2023–2024 panels).
- **Official quality warnings:** The Bureau published a "2023 SIPP: Insufficient Geographic Coverage and Unit Nonresponse" user note, and the 2024 Release Notes warn of "data collection complications because of increasing costs and a general lower-than-average unit response rate."
- **Lost waves:** The 2019 panel was discontinued after Wave 1; multiple waves in the 2020–2022 panels were de-prioritized or zeroed out (see the 2024 Users' Guide panel table showing "0" person counts for several waves).
- **Planned granularity/frequency changes:** The 2027 redesign shifts to a six-month reference period, a new single-respondent household design, and "alternative sample and weighting methodologies" — a fundamental break in comparability with the 2014–2025 series, in addition to the skipped collection year (a frequency reduction).

**Evidence for "Moderate Risk" (mitigating):**
- The Bureau is actively investing in remedies (multi-mode collection, administrative-records imputation, SIPP Seamless year-round interviewing), and annual releases continue with full documentation, crosswalks, and user notes — transparency about quality problems remains high.

**Assessment: High Risk.** Reductions in effective granularity (sample size, geographic reliability, lost panels/waves) are documented and current, not merely potential — and an announced frequency break arrives in 2027.

---

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence for "No Known Issue":**
- **Explicit statutory authorization:** Title 13 U.S.C. §182 explicitly authorizes the Census Bureau to conduct surveys like SIPP, with Title 13's confidentiality protections attached.
- **Required for statutory reporting:** CBPP (September 2025) confirms SIPP "is the only nationally representative survey of its size that tracks how long people receive various government benefits. **This information is required for annual reports to Congress under federal law**" (welfare-dependence and program-participation reporting originating in PRWORA 1996).
- **No substitutes:** No alternative collection replicates SIPP's monthly longitudinal income, program-participation spells, and intra-year family dynamics. The administration's proposed administrative-records approach has been assessed by CBPP and the National Academies as incapable of replicating this content.
- **Program implementation:** SIPP feeds SSA's MINT model, CBO models, and USDA SNAP eligibility models used to implement and cost federal programs.

**Evidence for "Moderate Risk":**
- SIPP is not mandated *by name* in statute; §182 is discretionary authority ("as necessary"), meaning an administration can legally scale it back without congressional action — as the 2027 field-test substitution demonstrates.

**Assessment: No Known Issue.** The statutory authorization is explicitly named, downstream statutory reporting requirements depend on it, and no substitute collection exists. Note, however, that this strong statutory footing did not prevent the announced collection skip — a gap worth flagging to policymakers.

---

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence for "High Risk":**
- **Staff losses ≥1,000:** AFGE reports the Census Bureau lost **at least 1,300 employees** since January 2025, mostly via deferred resignation and early retirement (GovExec, July 2025) — exceeding the rubric's 1,000-person High Risk trigger. The American Statistical Association estimates a ~15% staffing decline since FY2024.
- **Leadership instability:** The Bureau has been under acting leadership for roughly 18 months (GovExec, July 2026); at least five division/office chiefs departed in early 2025 (NPR, April 2025).
- The FY2026 President's Budget requested Current Demographic Statistics (SIPP's line) at $73M — a **$40M (~35%) cut** from the $113M actual level — and proposed a 27% staffing cut for periodic programs.

**Evidence for "Moderate Risk" (mitigating):**
- The enacted FY2026 bill (P.L. 119-74) rejected the deep cut: Current Surveys and Programs received $318.5M, only **–3.2%** vs. FY2025, and the overall Bureau budget rose 7.8%. Congress's action blunted the worst funding scenario.
- Percentage staff loss (~10–15%) falls in the Moderate band, and losses were bureau-wide rather than targeted at the SIPP division.

**Assessment: High Risk.** Applying the rubric's "and/or" logic, the loss of 1,300+ staff (≥1,000) alone meets the High Risk threshold, compounded by prolonged acting leadership and a (rejected but revealing) proposed 35% cut to SIPP's budget line. The enacted appropriation is genuinely mitigating and is the main reason this is not worse.

---

## 6. Policy

**Evidence for "High Risk":**
- **Official administration criticism of the survey:** The FY2026 Congressional Budget Justification singles out SIPP as "expensive and challenging for respondents," proposes "transitioning to a more effective approach that merges modern survey techniques with advanced data science methods," a "smaller, more targeted sample," and "non survey data to lower costs" — and pointedly does not confirm the program will continue under its current name (Census Project, June 30, 2025).
- **Significant change in motion, aligned with administration priorities:** The August 2026 Federal Register notice operationalizes that vision — substituting a 6,000-person field test for the national collection and redesigning the survey around internet self-response, administrative records, and new Bureau "Business Ecosystem" systems. This is an executed change, not merely a floated idea.
- **Context of parallel terminations:** USDA's September 2025 termination of the CPS Food Security Supplement (with rhetoric about "redundant, costly" data) shows the administration's willingness to eliminate adjacent income/wellbeing data collections, and the FY2026 budget proposed reorganizing BLS, BEA, and Census.

**Evidence for "Moderate Risk":**
- The field-test ICR is still pending OMB approval (comment period closed October 6, 2026), and the Bureau frames the changes as modernization rather than termination; Congress has pushed back on the funding side.

**Assessment: High Risk.** A formal budget document criticizing the dataset, a proposal to replace its core methodology, and a published ICR substituting a field test for national collection together constitute "other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities." This is beyond "proposed or pending" — the replacement process is underway.

## Summary of Risk Levels

| Category | Risk Level |
|---|---|
| Historical Data Availability | **No Known Issue** |
| Future Data Availability | **High Risk** |
| Data Quality | **High Risk** |
| Statutory Context | **No Known Issue** |
| Staffing and Funding | **High Risk** |
| Policy | **High Risk** |

**Overall interpretation:** SIPP presents an unusual risk profile. Its *historical archive* is intact and well-mirrored, and its *statutory footing* is strong — yet its *future* is among the most precarious of any major federal survey: a formally announced skip of the 2027 national collection, a workforce depleted by 1,300+ staff, acting leadership, documented quality erosion already in the public-use files, and an explicit administration plan to replace the survey's design with a cheaper administrative-records-based model. Congressional action in the FY2026 appropriations bill (restoring the proposed $40M cut) is the single most important mitigating factor and demonstrates that external advocacy can move outcomes. For preservationists: historical files are safe *today*, but the 2014–2025 design series may end with the 2026 release, making proactive archiving of current microdata, documentation, and crosswalks a time-sensitive priority.
